solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Passes such practical training (5-2)

blocks.note: passes as a verb: gives something along to the next person
training done by doing rather than by reading

annotation.surface: A trainee who gets through a practical course.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Passes' reads as exam success, fitting the training; it is really a two-word verb, HANDS ON, as in passing something along.
annotation.definitionFit: To hand something on is to pass it; hands-on training is the practical kind.

entries.clue: Slaves sneaked up after a horse (6)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, 'up' turns the word to read bottom to top
indicatorNotes.after: the reversed word comes after the horse

blocks.note: horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

annotation.surface: Slaves creeping up behind a horse, perhaps to escape.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Horse' is slang for heroin, and so H. Helots were the serf class of ancient Sparta.
annotation.definitionFit: Helots were the state-owned serfs of Sparta, so slaves.

entries.clue: Lawgiver’s original weight (6)

annotation.surface: Asks what weight a lawgiver originally carried.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lawgiver' suggests Moses or Solon; it is the scientist behind the laws of motion. There is a bonus: a newton is itself a unit of force, such as weight.
annotation.definitionFit: Isaac Newton gave physics its three laws of motion.

entries.clue: Crabby types, drunkenly egocentric in speech (9)

indicatorNotes.drunkenly: a drunk's tongue is loose, so every S he says comes out slurred as SH
indicatorNotes.in speech: the word is taken as it is spoken, not as it is spelt

blocks.note: egocentric = selfish; say it with a drunk's slur on each S

annotation.surface: Grumpy drunks who talk only about themselves.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crabby' looks like bad temper; it means crab-like. The sound change is the drunk's slur of S to SH.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: crabs, lobsters and prawns all belong to the hard-shelled sea creatures.

entries.clue: Devilishly enchanting concertina playing Mike interrupts (11)

indicatorNotes.playing: the concertina's letters are played about with
indicatorNotes.interrupts: M breaks into the rearranged letters

blocks.note: Mike is M in the radio alphabet

annotation.surface: A concertina player called Mike who breaks in with a bewitching tune.
annotation.walkthrough: Mike looks like a musician's name; it is the radio code word for M. Necromancy is magic by raising the dead, hence 'devilishly'.
annotation.definitionFit: Necromantic means working black magic, so devilishly enchanting.

entries.clue: Mistake to engage feeble reactionary (8)

indicatorNotes.to engage: BISH takes LIMP inside it, as in engaging gears

blocks.note: bish is British slang for a blunder

annotation.surface: Calls a feeble reactionary a mistake to hire.
annotation.walkthrough: Bish is dated British slang for a mistake. Colonel Blimp was a pompous, reactionary cartoon character, hence blimpish.
annotation.definitionFit: Blimpish, after the cartoon Colonel Blimp, means pompously reactionary.

entries.clue: For old chemist, too bad not to have these days back (4)

indicatorNotes.not to have: the letters for 'these days' are taken out

blocks.note: AD = anno Domini, our era, so 'these days'; removed

annotation.surface: A chemist of old lamenting that modern times have not come round again.
annotation.walkthrough: Jesse Boot built Boots, the British high-street chemist chain. AD, the present era, is lifted out of TOO BAD before the rest is reversed.
annotation.definitionFit: Jesse Boot, Lord Trent, was the pharmacist behind the Boots chemist chain.

entries.clue: Leader of worship welcomes wife with an ironically disbelieving expression (2,1,8)

indicatorNotes.welcomes: IMAM takes DUTCH in, as a host takes a guest

blocks.note: an imam leads prayers in a mosque
'my old Dutch' is Cockney slang for a wife

annotation.surface: An imam greeting a wife while pulling a sceptical face.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dutch' for wife is Cockney, from 'duchess'. 'If that's true, I'm a Dutchman' is how a Briton says they don't believe it.
annotation.definitionFit: 'I'm a Dutchman' follows a claim you think false, ironically scoffing at it.

entries.clue: The sole catlike creature in the house (11)

blocks.note: planta is the anatomical name for the sole of the foot
a genet is a spotted, cat-like mammal

annotation.surface: The only cat-like animal living in the house.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sole' reads as 'only'; it is the underside of the foot, whose Latin name PLANTA gives 'plantar'. The house is royal: the Plantagenets ruled England for three centuries.
annotation.definitionFit: The Plantagenets were a royal house of England from Henry II to Richard III.

entries.clue: Without moving, grabbing a bit of chocolate in a flash (9)

indicatorNotes.grabbing: STILL grabs C and IN inside it
indicatorNotes.a bit of: one letter of chocolate, its first

annotation.surface: Someone standing still, snatching a bit of chocolate in a split second.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In a flash' reads as 'instantly', but IN and A are wordplay and only 'flash' defines. A scintilla is literally a spark in Latin.
annotation.definitionFit: Scintilla is Latin for a spark, a flash of light; in English a tiny trace.

entries.clue: A pig died on the train (6)

blocks.note: a boar is a male pig
d. = died, as in family trees

annotation.surface: A pig that died on a train journey.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pins 'on the train' to the pig's death, but it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: passengers who have boarded any carriage, ship or aircraft are aboard.

entries.clue: Winger, British, to go without international selection (8)

blocks.note: to lack is to go without
a player picked for their country wins a cap

annotation.surface: A British winger left out of the national team.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Winger' belongs to football in the surface; it is a bird. A cap is awarded for each international appearance.
annotation.definitionFit: A crossword-only sense: anything with wings is a winger, and this warbler has a dark crown.

entries.clue: Where one has a subject mastered, makes up suggestions to drink a measure of spirits (2,4,10)

annotation.definition: Where one has a subject mastered

indicatorNotes.to drink: ATONES TIPS swallows FINGER between its two words

blocks.note: to atone is to make up for a wrong
a finger of whisky is a measure the width of a finger

annotation.surface: Someone apologising with advice to have a whisky.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Makes up' sounds like invention; it means making amends. A finger is a bar measure of spirits.
annotation.definitionFit: Knowledge at one's fingertips is fully mastered and ready to use.

entries.clue: Ruling line under empty diary, not pleasant (7)

indicatorNotes.under: in a down clue, NASTY sits below DY
indicatorNotes.empty: diary with its inside removed leaves D…Y

annotation.surface: An unpleasant rule of drawing a line beneath an empty diary.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ruling line' looks like a ruled line under the diary; it is a succession of rulers.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a succession of monarchs from one family, passing power down the generations.

entries.clue: On principle, feigned forbearance with which I answer Middle East expert (8,2,6)

indicatorNotes.On: the anagram goes on after LAW
indicatorNotes.feigned: the letters of forbearance are faked into a new order
indicatorNotes.with which: I and A are the things the forbearance comes with, added to its letters

annotation.surface: A pundit on the Middle East answering with feigned patience on principle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On principle' reads as 'as a matter of principle'; it puts the rest on LAW. T. E. Lawrence led the Arab Revolt of 1916–18.
annotation.definitionFit: T. E. Lawrence, 'of Arabia', was the British officer famed for his knowledge of the Arab world.

entries.clue: Book a benefit for stupid oaf (6)

annotation.surface: Booking a welfare payment for a fool.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a verb, to reserve; it is the noun, abbreviated B.
annotation.definitionFit: Baboon is an insult for a clumsy, stupid person.

entries.clue: What may be nuclear force covers a great distance to protect island (8)

indicatorNotes.covers: in a down clue, F sits on top of what follows
indicatorNotes.to protect: MILES wraps round I to shield it

blocks.note: miles = a great distance, as in 'miles away'

annotation.surface: A nuclear force that ranges far to defend an island.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nuclear force' reads as weapons, but 'force' belongs to the wordplay. A nuclear family is parents and children only.
annotation.definitionFit: Families of just parents and children are called nuclear families.

entries.clue: See you as well swallowing endlessly large amounts (6-2)

indicatorNotes.swallowing: TOO takes the other word inside it

blocks.note: oodles = large amounts; its end S is dropped

annotation.surface: A farewell, and a remark that someone ate a lot too.
annotation.walkthrough: TOODLE-OO is an old-fashioned, jaunty British goodbye.
annotation.definitionFit: Toodle-oo is a jaunty way to say goodbye, like 'see you'.

entries.clue: Performing couple warmer at night? Not very (4)

indicatorNotes.Not very: V, short for very, is taken out

blocks.note: a duvet keeps you warm in bed

annotation.surface: A couple asking whether a duvet keeps them warm at night, and hearing: not very.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not very' reads as the answer to a question; it is the instruction to drop V from DUVET.
annotation.definitionFit: A duet is a performance by two, or the pair performing it.

entries.clue: Unprofitable? This joint succeeded, for one (9)

indicatorNotes.for: ANKLES stands in for the I of THIS

blocks.note: I = one, the letter it replaces

annotation.surface: Asks whether a joint venture that succeeded could still be unprofitable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For one' looks like 'for example'; it means 'in place of I'. So THIS swaps its I for ANKLE + S.
annotation.definitionFit: A thankless task earns no reward, so it is unprofitable.

entries.clue: Clock sounds after seconds not moving (8)

indicatorNotes.after: 'after' means following in order, so in a down clue the clock sounds sit below S

blocks.note: ticking is the sound a clock makes

annotation.surface: A clock still ticking just after its hands have stopped.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is all clocks, so 'seconds' reads as time passing; it just gives S.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a drawer or door that is sticking is jammed fast and won't budge.

entries.clue: For very big performance an endless check (8)

blocks.note: a tick is a check mark; its end K is dropped

annotation.surface: A spot check that never ends before a huge show.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Check' could be a restraint or an inspection; it is the tick mark.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from the giants of Greek myth: enormous, huge, colossal.

entries.clue: I am frugally treated in miscellaneous gathering (11)

indicatorNotes.treated: the letters are processed into a new form

annotation.surface: A guest complaining of being fed stingily at a mixed get-together.
annotation.walkthrough: A gallimaufry is a jumble or hotchpotch, from an old French word for a stew of leftovers.
annotation.definitionFit: A gallimaufry is a medley, a miscellaneous jumble of things.

entries.clue: Obvious mate approaching White capturing bishop (8)

indicatorNotes.approaching: PAL comes just before the next part
indicatorNotes.capturing: PALE takes B inside, as a chess piece takes another

blocks.note: B is bishop in chess notation

annotation.surface: A chess commentator: obvious mate coming for White, who takes the bishop.
annotation.walkthrough: The chess surface makes 'mate' checkmate and 'White' a player; they are a friend and a colour.
annotation.definitionFit: Palpable means able to be felt, so plainly evident, obvious.

entries.clue: Query order to appear for examination (4,4,8)

blocks.note: to query something is to call it into question
read literally: summon someone in to be questioned

annotation.surface: Challenging a summons to appear for an exam.
annotation.walkthrough: The second meaning takes the phrase literally: call a person in for questioning.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to cast doubt on a claim, and read literally, to summon someone in for questioning.

entries.clue: A touch frantic, not cold and listless (9)

indicatorNotes.not: 'not cold' means without cold, so the C that stands for cold is taken away

blocks.note: a pat is a light touch
c = cold, as on taps; removed

annotation.surface: Someone a bit frantic, yet not unwell and lethargic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A touch' looks like 'slightly'; it is A + PAT. The frantic word loses one of its two Cs, the first.
annotation.definitionFit: Apathetic means lacking interest or energy, listless.

entries.clue: Chap taking a risk cut tongue (8)

indicatorNotes.taking: MAN takes the next part on after it

blocks.note: taking a risk = daring; its end G is cut

annotation.surface: A man who takes a risk and has his tongue cut.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tongue' is a language, not an organ.
annotation.definitionFit: Mandarin is the main language of China, and tongue means language.

entries.clue: Be aware of master of trivia’s return (4)

indicatorNotes.return: the word comes back the other way

blocks.note: a wonk is an expert obsessed with detail

annotation.surface: A quiz champion who knows a thing or two coming back.
annotation.walkthrough: A wonk knows every detail of a subject, often a dull one.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: having information or understanding in your head about a fact.

entries.clue: When initially a peerage cropped up, did one sleep on it? (8)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition is a question about the answer: a waterbed is the thing one sleeps on

indicatorNotes.initially: only the first letter of When
indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, the letters read upwards

blocks.note: Debrett's Peerage is the guide to the British aristocracy; its end T goes

annotation.surface: Wondering whether someone who suddenly got a peerage stayed awake over it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Peerage' names the reference book, Debrett's, which lists Britain's titled families. 'Sleep on it' also means to delay a decision, the surface's reading.
annotation.definitionFit: A waterbed is a bed with a water-filled mattress, something one sleeps on.

entries.clue: The lowdown from inside grand opera … (4)

indicatorNotes.from inside: the answer lies within the words that follow

annotation.surface: Inside gossip from backstage at the opera.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue runs on into 30 down, where 'one' means an opera.
annotation.definitionFit: Dope is slang for inside information, the lowdown.

entries.clue: Destroy books, trashy magazines and film (4,7)

blocks.note: to pulp is to mash up, destroy

annotation.surface: A call to pulp books, trashy magazines and a film.
annotation.walkthrough: Three layers: the wordplay, cheap pulp magazines, and Tarantino's 1994 film named after them.
annotation.definitionFit: Pulp fiction is lurid writing on cheap paper, and the title of Tarantino's film.

entries.clue: … a piece of information following part of one (4)

indicatorNotes.following: a word that gives F, not a positional instruction

blocks.note: 'one' is the grand opera from 28 down, and an act is part of it

annotation.surface: Continues 28 down: the gossip is a piece of news about part of the opera.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Following' looks like a placement instruction; here it is the abbreviation F. 'One' reaches back to the opera in 28 down.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: one true, known detail, the kind a reference book lists.

entries.clue: Attend to his desperate cry of failure (5,4,2)

indicatorNotes.desperate: the letters are in a wild state and rearranged

annotation.surface: Urging someone to answer a man's desperate cry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Desperate' seems to describe the cry; it works on the three words before it.
annotation.definitionFit: 'That's done it!' is what you say when something has gone irretrievably wrong.

entries.clue: As OAP, I don’t fancy taking on children (8)

indicatorNotes.fancy: the letters are made into something elaborate

annotation.surface: A pensioner who has no wish to take on children.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' reads as a verb, to want; it is the anagram instruction. OAP means old-age pensioner.
annotation.definitionFit: Adoption is legally taking on another's children as your own.

entries.clue: In races on slope beside river these are taken off balance (4,7)

blocks.note: a river bank is a sloping edge
to charge in is to race in

annotation.surface: Horses racing down a riverside slope and losing their footing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Off balance' sounds like tottering; it means deducted from an account's balance.
annotation.definitionFit: Bank charges are fees deducted from the balance of your account.

entries.clue: Everyone you said to call is seductive (8)

indicatorNotes.said: you is taken as spoken, sounding like the letter U

blocks.note: to ring is to call on the phone

annotation.surface: Telling everyone that a phone call from you is seductive.
annotation.walkthrough: Every part is a simple swap; the surface turns them into a flirt's compliment.
annotation.definitionFit: Alluring means attractive, tempting, seductive.

entries.clue: Put weight behind reflective backing track (11)

indicatorNotes.Put: an instruction to place the weight somewhere, with 'behind' saying where
indicatorNotes.behind: behind means following, so in a down clue the weight sits below the backing

blocks.note: silvering is the reflective coat on the back of a mirror
a stone is a British weight of 14 pounds

annotation.surface: Musicians throwing their weight behind a thoughtful backing track.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backing track' is a musical phrase; the words split, with 'track' the definition. Silverstone is the motor-racing circuit that hosts the British Grand Prix.
annotation.definitionFit: Silverstone is a motor-racing track in Northamptonshire.

entries.clue: Sellers say first to engage punter is to gain advantage (2,3,6)

indicatorNotes.first to: only the first letter of engage

blocks.note: Peter Sellers was one of the Goons, of radio's The Goon Show

annotation.surface: Salespeople's tip: hook the customer first to gain the upper hand.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sellers' reads as salespeople, with 'punter' as the customer; Sellers is Peter Sellers, one of The Goon Show's comedians.
annotation.definitionFit: To go one better is to outdo someone, gaining the advantage.

entries.clue: Language students finally losing memory spoil one answer (11)

indicatorNotes.finally: only the last letter of losing

annotation.surface: Language students who, at the end, lose their memory and ruin an answer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Language students finally' reads as one phrase; the break falls after 'students', and 'finally' works on 'losing'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: scholars whose subject is how sentences are built, its syntax and word forms.

entries.clue: Mainly regret I abandoned rewritten film (5,6)

indicatorNotes.abandoned: I is dropped from the letters
indicatorNotes.rewritten: the rest are written out again in a new order

annotation.surface: A screenwriter mostly regretting giving up on a rewrite.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mainly' looks like 'mostly' qualifying regret; it is fodder. Elmer Gantry is a 1960 film of Sinclair Lewis's novel about a con-man preacher.
annotation.definitionFit: Elmer Gantry (1960) won Burt Lancaster an Oscar in the title role.

entries.clue: A little heterosexual love personified (4)

indicatorNotes.A little: a small part of the next word

annotation.surface: A touch of straight love, embodied.
annotation.walkthrough: Eros, the Greek god of love, hides in a word that already has love in its sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of love, love in person.

entries.clue: Craft group regularly full on up to start of autumn (8)

indicatorNotes.regularly: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so take letters at a steady step: every other one

annotation.surface: A craft club meeting regularly until the autumn.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Craft group' reads as knitting circles; craft here means boats.
annotation.definitionFit: A flotilla is a small fleet, a group of boats.

entries.clue: Explain reason for delayed arrival? Not I (9)

indicatorNotes.Not: 'not I' means the phrase without I, so that letter is left out

blocks.note: 'train's late' is why you arrive late

annotation.surface: A commuter's excuse for arriving late: not my fault.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not I' reads as 'not me'; it removes I from TRAIN'S LATE.
annotation.definitionFit: To translate can mean to explain or interpret in plainer terms.

entries.clue: Put out about mistake getting such lengthy exposure (4-5)

indicatorNotes.about: 'about' as in 'about turn': the word faces the other way

blocks.note: to emit is to put out

annotation.surface: A photographer upset at a mistake that left the shutter open too long.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put out' looks like 'annoyed'; it means emit. 'Such' makes the answer describe the kind of exposure.
annotation.definitionFit: Time-lapse photography uses long-spaced exposures, compressing hours into seconds.

entries.clue: At uni, sail horribly fateful vessel (9)

annotation.surface: A student at university sailing badly.
annotation.walkthrough: The Lusitania was the liner sunk by a German U-boat in 1915.
annotation.definitionFit: The liner Lusitania was torpedoed in 1915, a fateful loss.

entries.clue: Was not one of the crowd plucky to arrest old con? (5,3)

annotation.definition: Was not one of the crowd

indicatorNotes.to arrest: STOUT holds O and DO inside it

blocks.note: to do someone is to con them

annotation.surface: A brave bystander who stepped forward to arrest an old conman.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old con' reads as a former convict; it is O + DO. Stout means brave as well as fat.
annotation.definitionFit: To stand out is to be conspicuous, not part of the crowd.

entries.clue: It may be on the bed against the window (11)

annotation.definition: It may be on the bed

blocks.note: a pane is a window's glass

annotation.surface: Something placed on a bed pushed up against the window.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface has the bed against the window; 'against the window' is the wordplay alone.
annotation.definitionFit: A counterpane is a bedspread, lying on top of the bed.

entries.clue: Willing extra fish in frozen condition to be docked (7)

indicatorNotes.to be docked: icily loses its last letter, as a tail is docked

blocks.note: icily = in a frozen way; its end Y is docked

annotation.surface: A spare frozen fish, willingly given, waiting to come into dock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Willing' looks like 'eager'; it means making a will. 'Docked' looks nautical; it means cut short.
annotation.definitionFit: A crossword-only sense: 'willing' means will-making, and this document is a supplement added after signing.

entries.clue: Virtually daily event is no more, sadly (8)

indicatorNotes.sadly: the letters are in a sorry state and rearranged

annotation.surface: An almost daily fixture that has, alas, ended.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Virtually' is exact: the moon rises about 50 minutes later each day, so some days have no moonrise at all.
annotation.definitionFit: The moon rises nearly every day, but on about one day a month it does not.

entries.clue: Nothing in copse to show track (6)

indicatorNotes.in: 'nothing in copse' puts the nothing inside the copse, as a letter placed within a word

blocks.note: a grove is a small wood, a copse

annotation.surface: An empty copse with no path through it.
annotation.walkthrough: A groove is also a record's track, which the surface leaves unsaid.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a cut channel or rut, including the spiral one on a vinyl record.

entries.clue: Having gathered sail, put off returning across centre of Med (6)

indicatorNotes.returning: DEFER comes back the other way
indicatorNotes.across: the reversed word spans the E
indicatorNotes.centre of: the centre of a word is its middle, so Med gives up its middle letter

blocks.note: to defer is to put off

annotation.surface: A sailor who took in sail and postponed the trip back across the Mediterranean.
annotation.walkthrough: To reef is to reduce a sail's area by gathering part of it in.
annotation.definitionFit: Reefing a sail means rolling or gathering part of it in.

entries.clue: Record increases, not much at first, lead to offers of savings (9)

indicatorNotes.not: 'not much' means without much's letter, so it is removed
indicatorNotes.at first: the first letter of much, M

blocks.note: its first letter, removed from MOUNTS

annotation.surface: Record sales rising slowly at first, leading to money-off offers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not much at first' reads as 'slowly to begin with'; it tells you to lose M, the first letter of much, from MOUNTS.
annotation.definitionFit: Discounts are reductions in price, offering savings.

entries.clue: Dress Cleopatra’s maid put back (4)

indicatorNotes.put back: to put something back is to send it the way it came, so the name reads backwards

blocks.note: Iras is Cleopatra's attendant in Shakespeare

annotation.surface: Cleopatra's maid putting a dress back on.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dress' reads as a verb for the maid's job; it is the noun. Iras dies alongside Cleopatra in Antony and Cleopatra.
annotation.definitionFit: A sari is the draped dress worn in South Asia.

entries.clue: Nameless colleague really missing helper to make beds (8)

annotation.definitionNote: a parterre is one garden made of many beds; the clue gives what it is made of

indicatorNotes.Nameless: without a name, so the N that abbreviates name is taken out
indicatorNotes.missing: the helper's letters are taken out

blocks.note: a partner is a colleague; N (name) goes
an ally is a helper; removed

annotation.surface: A colleague with no helper really has to make the beds alone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Make beds' sounds like housework; the beds are for flowers. A parterre is a formal garden of ornamental beds.
annotation.definitionFit: A parterre is a formal arrangement of ornamental flower beds.

entries.clue: Without hesitation think about garden feature (4)

indicatorNotes.Without: 'without hesitation' means lacking the hesitant ER, so it is left out

blocks.note: to ponder is to think about

annotation.surface: Considering a garden pond without dithering.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Without hesitation' looks like 'decisively'; it strips ER from PONDER.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a small pool of still water is one ornament a landscaped plot may have.

entries.clue: A sometimes prominent feature too big for trousers (6)

blocks.note: a chin is a facial feature that can jut out

annotation.surface: A bulge that is too big for someone's trousers.
annotation.walkthrough: OS is the British clothing label for outsize.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: casual cotton twill slacks, first made for army uniforms.

entries.clue: From censor that “No” outrageous: lid put on popular play (3,2,1,3,3,4)

annotation.answer: CAT ON A HOT TIN ROOF

indicatorNotes.outrageous: the letters of 'that no' go wild
indicatorNotes.put on: a lid is put on top of a pot; in an across entry, 'on' places the lid next to, and after, popular

blocks.note: Cato the Censor, the stern Roman statesman
a roof is a lid over a building

annotation.surface: A censor's outrageous 'no' slapped on a popular play.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Censor' reads as the official who banned plays; it is the Roman Cato. Tennessee Williams's play did in fact meet censors on stage and screen.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Tennessee Williams's 1955 Pulitzer-winning drama about Brick, Maggie and Big Daddy.

entries.clue: Extension — does one go on at it? (6)

annotation.definition2: does one go on at it?
annotation.definitionNote: the second definition is a question whose answer is the phrase 'at length'

blocks.note: extension as extent: how far something reaches

blocks.clueFragment: does one go on at it?
blocks.note: think of the idiom for talking too long: one goes on 'at ...'

annotation.surface: An extension, and a query about whether one waffles.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half is a cryptic hint: someone who talks too much goes on 'at length'.
annotation.definitionFit: Length is extension in space; one who rambles goes on at length.

entries.clue: Made available free (8)

blocks.note: as a film or record is put out to the public
free as a verb in the past: let out, as a prisoner is

annotation.walkthrough: 'Free' also suggests 'no charge', which fits 'made available' in the wrong way.
annotation.definitionFit: Released means both put on sale or show and set free.

entries.clue: With November moving on a bit, longed for December (4,3)

indicators: With November moving on a bit

indicatorNotes.With November moving on a bit: November is N in the radio alphabet, and moving it on a bit shifts that one letter a couple of places along

blocks.note: longed = yearned; its N then moves on two places

annotation.surface: Someone who, as November wore on, longed for December.
annotation.walkthrough: November here is the letter N, not the month; moving it two places turns YEARNED into YEAREND.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the twelfth month closes the calendar, so it is the final stretch of it.
